history.title: Follow the Decision

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Somebody decided where the crosswalk goes. Somebody decided when the library closes. This week you find out who, and how ordinary people get those decisions changed.

1. Read **Who Decided That?**
2. Learn the words in **Town Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Three Levels, One Question** chart open.
4. Fill in **Town Cornell Notes** as you read.
5. Sort the cards in **Who Decides This?**
6. Take **Town Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Levels**.
8. Read **Town Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Propose: One Change to Your Town**.

Your job this week: find one rule in your town and try to work out who made it. 🏛️

history.title: Who Decided That?
history.data:
## Who Decided That?

There is a crosswalk near your school. Somebody decided to put it there. Somebody decided what time the library closes, and whether the park gets a new slide.

Those were real decisions, made by real people, in a meeting you were allowed to attend.

**Government** happens at three levels. The national level handles things like the army and money. The state level handles things like driver's licences and most school rules. The **local** level is your city or town, and it handles a surprising amount of what you actually touch: parks, libraries, rubbish collection, crosswalks, fire stations.

Most towns are run by a **council**, a small group of people **citizens** elect. Many also elect a **mayor** to lead. The council passes an **ordinance**, which is the word for a rule made by a town rather than a state or a country.

The council also sets a **budget**, and this is where the real decisions live. A town has only so much money. Spending it on one **service** means not spending it on another. A new library roof might mean waiting another year for the skate park. Nobody is being mean. The money simply ran out, and somebody had to choose.

So how does anything change?

Council meetings are open to the public, and most set aside time for anyone to speak. People sign a **petition**, a written request with many names on it, to show a lot of people want the same thing. And people **vote**, which is the slowest tool and the strongest one.

Now the part that surprises people. Far fewer people vote in local elections than in national ones. In many places, well under half of those who could vote actually do, and in some local elections it is under a quarter.

That matters more than it sounds. It means local decisions — the ones closest to your street — are often made by a small number of people who showed up. A room with twenty people in it can change a town.

Which is the good news and the bad news at once. The people who show up decide. And you can be one of them, sooner than you think.

data.instructions: Two cards hold the big ideas. Study the example, make one your own, and say how it helps you.

essentialFacts: The national level handles things like the army and money.

cards.aiExample: Three rings around your house. The inner ring is your town. The middle ring is your state. The outer ring is the country. The closer the ring, the more it touches your day.
cards.mapping: Distance on the picture matches distance in real life, so the ring you can almost step into is the one you can actually walk into.
cards.scaffoldStarter: Inner ring: ____. Middle ring: ____. Outer ring: ____.
scaffoldSteps: Draw three rings around your home.
Put one level on each ring.
Name one thing each level decides.
cards.studentPrompt: Draw your own picture of the three levels.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Why is the nearest ring the easiest one to change?

hookFact.text: A room with twenty people in it can change a town.

cards.target: Why a budget is a set of choices, not a list
essentialFacts: A town has only so much money.
Spending on one service means not spending on another.
A new library roof might mean waiting another year for the skate park.
cards.aiExample: A budget is like one pizza at a party. Every slice you hand to somebody is a slice nobody else gets. The argument is never about the pizza. It is about the slices.
cards.mapping: A pizza is obviously finite, which is the one feature of a budget that people forget when they ask why the town cannot just do both.
cards.scaffoldStarter: The town chose ____. That means ____ had to wait.
scaffoldSteps: Name something a town might fund.
Name what it would have to wait for.
Say who is affected by each.
coachPrompts: Who gets asked about the slice that was not handed out?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own comparison for a budget.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Why is asking what got left out a better question than asking what got funded?

history.title: Town Check

questions.question: Which level of government most likely decided where your crosswalk goes?
options: The national level, since roads cross the country
The local level, since it handles streets and crossings
The state level, since it sets all the speed limits
No level; a road company decides that by itself
questions.correctAnswer: The local level, since it handles streets and crossings

questions.question: What is an ordinance?
options: A rule made by a town rather than a state
A plan for how a town will spend its money
A written request signed by many people
A meeting that is open to the public
questions.correctAnswer: A rule made by a town rather than a state

questions.question: Why does the reading say the budget is where the real decisions live?
options: Because budgets are written in very difficult language
Because the mayor writes it without asking anybody
Because money is limited, so funding one thing means not another
Because it is the only document the public may read
questions.correctAnswer: Because money is limited, so funding one thing means not another
questions.conceptLabel: a budget is a set of choices

questions.question: Which is described as the slowest tool and the strongest one?
options: Signing a petition with many names on it
Speaking at the public time in a meeting
Writing a letter to the local newspaper
Voting in an election when one comes round
questions.correctAnswer: Voting in an election when one comes round

questions.question: Fewer people vote in local elections than national ones. Why does that matter?
options: It means local elections do not really count for much
It means a small number of people decide nearby things
It means the state has to step in and decide instead
It means local elections are held less often than others
questions.correctAnswer: It means a small number of people decide nearby things
questions.conceptLabel: the people who show up decide

questions.question: Name three ways an ordinary person can try to change a local rule, and say which is slowest.
questions.expectedAnswer: Speak during the public time at a council meeting, sign or start a petition, and vote in local elections. Voting is the slowest, because you have to wait for an election, but the reading calls it the strongest.

questions.question: A town funds a new library roof this year. What question does the reading say you should ask next?
questions.expectedAnswer: Ask what got left out. Because the money is limited, funding the roof means something else had to wait, such as the skate park. Looking at what was not funded tells you as much as looking at what was.

history.title: Town Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Can a kid actually speak at a council meeting? 🎤
data.answer: In most towns, yes. Public comment time is usually open to anyone who lives there, whatever their age. Some councils ask you to sign up first. It is worth checking your town's website.

data.question: Do petitions ever work?
data.answer: Sometimes. A petition does not force anyone to act. What it does is show that many people want the same thing, which is hard to ignore in a small town. It works best alongside showing up.

data.question: Why are local elections held on odd days? 🗳️
data.answer: Many towns hold them separately from national ones, often in spring or in odd-numbered years. Researchers think this is part of why turnout is so low, because fewer people notice they are happening.

data.question: What if the council decides something unfair?
data.answer: People can speak against it, organise, vote the members out at the next election, and in some cases challenge it in court if it conflicts with state or national law.

data.question: Who pays for the library and the park? 💰
data.answer: Mostly local taxes, often on property, plus some money passed down from the state. That is why the budget argument is really an argument about how much everyone contributes and what it buys.

data.question: Is a mayor the boss of everything?
data.answer: Not usually. Towns are set up differently. In many, the council holds most of the power and the mayor leads meetings. In others the mayor runs daily business. It is worth finding out which yours is.

data.title: One Change to Your Town
data.instructions: Pick one thing you would change locally. Work out who actually decides it, what it would cost, and what would have to wait. Then write the proposal.
data.fitReason: The standard asks students to explain how people change rules and laws. Making them identify the right level and name a tradeoff turns a wish into a proposal, which is the difference the reading is built on.

brief.context: Your class is making a display for the school entrance called One Change. Each team picks something real about the town: a crossing, a park, library hours, a bus stop, a bike lane.
brief.audience: Your town council, who read short proposals from the public
brief.drivingQuestion: What is one change worth asking for, who exactly has the power to make it, and what would the town have to give up to pay for it?
brief.seedDirection: Work out the level first. If it turns out to be a state decision, either pick something else or say plainly who you would have to reach instead.
lockedLessonFacts: The local level handles parks, libraries, rubbish and crosswalks.
A council passes ordinances and sets a budget.
A town has only so much money, so funding one service means not funding another.
People change things by speaking at meetings, by petition, and by voting.
openQuestions: Is this really a local decision, or does it belong to another level?
Who benefits, and is there anyone it would inconvenience?
What would you be willing to see wait so this could happen?
stakeholders: Neighbours who benefit from the change
Anyone who loses out if money moves
criteria: The change is named clearly, in one sentence
The correct level of government is identified, with a reason
A rough cost is estimated, and one thing that would have to wait is named
One person or group who might object is named, and answered
At least four glossary words used correctly
constraints: It must be something a council could actually do
One page, because that is what gets read
brief.deliverable: A one-page proposal: the change, the level and why, a rough cost, what would have to wait, and your answer to the strongest objection.

parallelExample.context: A team wanted the school day to start later and wrote it as a town proposal.
parallelExample.move: They found that school hours are set by the district and the state, not the council. Rather than dropping it, they rewrote the proposal to the school board and said in one line why the council was the wrong audience.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Finding the right level was the whole difference between a complaint and a proposal that could actually be acted on.

supports.frameStarter: We propose ____. This is a ____ decision because ____. It would cost about ____, which means ____ would wait.
frameChoices: A bench or shelter at the bus stop
A bike lane on one street
coachPrompts: Did you check which level actually decides this?

Who would object, and what would you say to them?
